newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In Grinning and baring it for freedom.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In Grinning and baring it for freedom.

text.p: If a student turned to the Internet to research the work "Little Women," she might end up unearthing a slew of sites that had nothing to do with the classic work but a lot more to do with the dark underside of the Net.

And thanks to the U.S. Supreme Court's decision last Thursday that struck down a law making it a crime to transmit sexually explicit material to anyone under 18, these kinds of pornographic sites can only multiply in cyberspace.
But is this such a terrible thing? Of course, many believe we should be concerned about our children stumbling on to what President Bill Clinton called the "red light districts of cyberspace."

The Supreme Court ruling perhaps summed it up the best when it said: "The interest in encouraging freedom of expression in a democratic society outweighs any theoretical but unproven benefit of censorship."

Now President Clinton and Bill Gates of Microsoft are suggesting that the better way to protect the young from some of the seemingly horrifying material freely available on the Internet is to use technological rather than legal means.

There are a number of proven technologies to help protect children, including using off-the-shelf programs that prevent browsers from going to sites that contain key words that parents find objectionable. And, of course, there are a number of low-tech methods such as instituting password protections on computers and, even more simply, not allowing children to use the family computer without adult supervision.

Of course, many of today's Net-savvy children can no doubt find their way through just about any porno fire walls put up by their parents, but that can be said of just about any of the controls used to protect minors from watching explicit television shows or viewing adult magazines. There are limits to what governments, society and even parents can do to protect the young and innocent.

But even if the censorship provisions of the Communications Decency Act won the blessing from the U.S. courts, it would have been a nightmare to enforce. Just how would have the courts enforced decency laws on the Net when it is so easy to host objectionable material in countries where there are no such laws on the books?

This does not mean that the Internet is above all laws or that it should be allowed to become the Wild Wide Web with absolutely no checks and balances. But we have to remember the Web is really as wide and wonderful as life itself and sometimes as bad and scary as life itself.

And so what about our mythical student (which was drawn from an actual experience)? Would she have encountered nothing but evil in her innocent search on "Little Women?" Maybe with a little supervision or ingenuity or even good luck, she might have found something of value on the Net for her research.

Perhaps she would have stumbled on a page at the Atlantic Monthly site (http://www.theatlantic.com/unbound/classrev/littlewo.htm) which contained a 1903 review by H.W. Boynton of Louisa May Alcott's "Little Women" book.

It opened with these lines: "There is, in short, no separate standard of taste by which to determine the value of books written for children. To be of permanent use, they must possess literary quality; that is, they must be whole-souled, broad, mature in temper, however simple they may need to be in theme or manner."
In the end, we can only hope works of poor quality will be temporal and those of permanent use, whether on paper or on the Net, will live through the ages for all ages.
